I'll mine the `ls -l` listings first, then go on to sorries. Checking the server's timezone and what the listings look like, since `ls` prints local time and the transcripts use UTC:Only 16 listings name memory files, and they add nothing. Checking why, starting with the Aug 30 listing I spotted earlier:Listings are in (`b64aa43`). Now milestone 3, sorries. First I'm reading how futon3c and futon2 already represent a challenged memory, so I don't add a second vocabulary:Smoke test on four pairs with `claude -p` and Haiku: two likely duplicates, the possible codex conflict, and the termux/phone1 pair.The judge works on all four: two duplicates (`restates`) and two `replaces`, each backed by quotes that check out verbatim. Both `replaces` are real staleness:
- `phone1-usb-ssd-blocked` says "A real mount is impossible", which the newer termux memory overturns.
- `codex-default-model-astra` says other seats "are still on the astra default", which the 09-27 memory about seat config contradicts.

Each call took 6–7 s; one took 59 s.

㊥ (milestone 3 so far) The `ls -l` listings are committed (`b64aa43`). They're real evidence but thin: only 16 listings name memory files, so just 2 memories start earlier, one back to Aug 30. For sorries, candidate selection and the judge both work. Running the judge over every pair is the remaining step, and it needs a model.

㊢ (pieces)
- **`scripts/candidates.py`** picks 631 pairs with no model involved: [[link]] pairs, plus pairs that share rare terms such as ports, repo names, device names and config paths.
- **`scripts/judge.py`** asks for one of the spec's verdicts (conflict / restates / replaces / unrelated). A verdict only counts if both quotes appear verbatim in the memories.

🈸 (one decision: which model judges the full 631 pairs)
1. **Haiku via `claude -p`.** About 75 minutes run one at a time, less in parallel. It uses a little of your subscription quota and sends memory text to Anthropic, which is no different from me reading it.
2. **Local GLM-Air.** The model files and `llama-server` binary survived the rebuild, but it isn't running. It needs about 70 GB of RAM and most of the cores, in its own systemd scope. At about 4 tokens/s, I'd estimate 8–10 hours. That's an overnight load on the shared box, so I'd rather you okay it.

My lean is option 1 now, with the judge left switchable so a local run can replace it later. Meanwhile I'll write the loader: conflicts become sorries in futon1b (a challenge that names both memories, using futon3c's `:challenged` vocabulary), duplicates become `:memory/restates` edges, and replacements become proposed supersessions rather than applied ones, since a model made the call.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-15
previous_reply_acts.text:
(what was added)
- **Existence markers.** A version with no text means the memory existed then but its content wasn't recovered. One goes before the first known version when there's earlier evidence the file existed:
  - its birth time on the old disk;
  - its name in non-error tool output;
  - its line in the memory index loaded at session start.
- **Unknown spans.** One also goes at a shell edit I can't read, when the text differs before and after it.
- **Claude Code's checkpoint backups** (`~/.claude/file-history/`) count as exact snapshots. When a backup says the file did not exist yet, that overrules any earlier claim that it existed.
- **Export.** `export-as-of` lists unknown-content memories in `UNKNOWN-CONTENT.txt`.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-15
previous_reply_acts.text: (precision bug, caught) The first run reported 7 contradictions and 271 markers. Both were caused by `stat %W` cutting birth times to whole seconds. The harness creates a memory file a few milliseconds after the tool call's timestamp, so a whole-second birth time looks earlier than the file's first version. With nanosecond birth times there are no contradictions and 123 markers. The contradiction check is what flagged it.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-15
previous_reply_acts.text:
(results)
- **Totals:** 515 versions, 141 of them unknown content: 123 before a first known version, 18 at unreadable shell edits.
- **09-15:** 100 files plus 15 known to exist with unknown content. Before this change it was 101 files and nothing else. The one fewer file is a memory whose text became unknown after a shell edit.
- **08-20:** 9 files plus 3 unknown.
- **Spot-check:** I traced three markers back to the records they cite and they were real.
- **Gates:** tests, clj-kondo and the parenthesis check all pass.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-15
previous_reply_acts.text: (why the gain is small) Transcripts start on 09-01. Old-disk birth times record the last write that replaced the file, not when it was created. So the median marker extends a memory's known start by 0 days.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-15
previous_reply_acts.text: (one more source, if wanted) The spot-check turned up a better source: `ls -l` output in transcripts. It records each listed file's modification time at the moment of listing, for example a 09-08 listing showing "Aug 30 10:14 server-remote-access-setup.md". Mining that would date existence back to late August for many files. It's small to add, and then milestone 3 (sorries) is next.
